title: WNBA and Players' Union Vow Action on Racist Abuse After Crisis Meeting
excerpt: Commissioner Cathy Engelbert met with WNBPA leadership to address death threats and racial slurs targeting players, pledging enhanced security as the league grapples with the dark side of its surging popularity.
body:
• The WNBA and its players' union are enhancing security measures in response to a rise in racist and abusive messages directed at players.
  • The crisis meeting was prompted by incidents of online abuse following a controversial game involving Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas.
  • Players like Alyssa Thomas and Chelsea Gray have publicly criticized the league's response to the threats and abuse they face.
  • The league acknowledges that receiving hateful messages has become a troubling norm for WNBA players.

The WNBA and its players' union issued a joint statement on Wednesday pledging to strengthen security measures after a high-level meeting to confront what both sides called a "recent increase in racist, hateful, and abusive messages directed at players."

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert and members of the Women's National Basketball Players Association's (WNBPA) executive committee and Justice, Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion (JEDI) committee met on Tuesday, July 21, ahead of the 2026 All-Star Game. League security officials were also present, according to USA Today.

What Sparked the Meeting

The WNBPA requested the meeting after weeks of escalating incidents. The flashpoint came on June 24, when Phoenix Mercury forward Alyssa Thomas made contact with Indiana Fever guard Caitlin Clark's throat during a Mercury win. The league upgraded the play to a Flagrant Foul 2 and suspended Thomas for one game.

https://x.com/SBJ/status/2080060955442970753

What followed was a deluge of online abuse. Thomas said she received death threats and racist messages, and publicly criticized Engelbert for staying silent.

"We still have yet to hear anything from Cathy. It's no surprise. You can see what's being said on social media... but as usual, she remains silent and that's unfortunate when our lives are being threatened. The league has to do better."

— Alyssa Thomas, Phoenix Mercury forward

Separately, Las Vegas Aces guard Chelsea Gray shared a screenshot of a racial slur she received on Instagram after a loss to the Fever on July 12. Fans quickly identified the sender as a Hilton Grand Vacations employee, and the company fired him within 48 hours for violating company policies.

Other players added their voices. Lynx guard Courtney Williams shared a homophobic audio message from a disgruntled sports bettor after a July 11 game. Natasha Cloud told Front Office Sports that receiving "racist, homophobic and hateful messages" had become "the new normal" for WNBA players.

What the League Promised

The joint statement described Tuesday's session as "an honest and meaningful conversation" and committed the league to "continuing to enhance security resources." The WNBA said it would partner with external organizations aligned with its values to advance player safety.

"Harassment, hate, none of that is okay. That goes for the opposing teams we play, that goes for my teammates, that goes for my coaches."

— Caitlin Clark, Indiana Fever guard

"Yesterday's discussion marked the beginning of an ongoing dialogue, and we are united in our commitment to building on this work together," the statement said, according to Reuters.

The WNBA had already launched a player safety program last year after players raised concerns that sexist and racist abuse had become an unwanted side effect of the league's rapid growth. Existing protocols include league and team security personnel who assess threats and coordinate with law enforcement. In March 2026, a new collective bargaining agreement between the WNBA and WNBPA included provisions for enhanced security, mental health resources, a stronger fan code of conduct, and an anti-hate campaign.

A Growing Pains Problem

NBA commissioner Adam Silver weighed in on July 17, calling Clark "a bit of a political football" and saying the situation was "incredibly unfair to her." Silver also acknowledged that WNBA officiating needs improvement, while declining to comment on reports that he personally pushed Engelbert to suspend Thomas.

The crisis illustrates a pattern common across global sports: explosive popularity bringing both revenue and toxicity. The WNBA's viewership and attendance have surged since Clark's arrival from Iowa in 2024, but the growth has attracted political tribalism and online vitriol that the league's infrastructure was not built to handle.

A Familiar Challenge for South Asian Sports Fans

For diaspora sports fans, the dynamic is recognizable. Indian cricket has grappled with similar issues — players like Mohammed Shami and Arshdeep Singh have faced communal abuse on social media after on-field results, prompting the BCCI to invest in cybersecurity and player wellness. The IPL's global audience, much like the WNBA's expanding fanbase, has forced administrators to reckon with the reality that bigger platforms mean bigger risks for the athletes on them.

The WNBA's challenge now is converting Tuesday's conversation into durable structural change — before the next incident forces another emergency meeting.
